children.text: T3: Glass ball

The first photograph shows a glass ball backlit with diffuse dichromatic light, containing only narrow spectral lines at red \(630\,\mathrm{nm}\) and violet \(400\,\mathrm{nm}\). The light comes from a white floor (marked 1) and white walls (marked 2), illuminated by violet and red LEDs. The camera sensor has red, green and blue sensors, so violet light appears blue. The camera distance is much greater than the ball radius.

children.text: A very narrow opaque thread is glued to the back surface along an arc of a great circle. The ball hides it from direct view, but strongly deformed images of a short thread segment appear as blue (b) and red (r) ellipses. The label p denotes purple areas. The ball centre is marked by a cross, its perimeter by a dashed line. The enlarged original photograph below is supplied for distance measurements and also traces the red-purple boundary.

The first photograph shows a glass ball backlit with diffuse dichromatic light, containing only narrow spectral lines at red \(630\,\mathrm{nm}\) and violet \(400\,\mathrm{nm}\). The light comes from a white floor (marked 1) and white walls (marked 2), illuminated by violet and red LEDs. The camera sensor has red, green and blue sensors, so violet light appears blue. The camera distance is much greater than the ball radius.

A very narrow opaque thread is glued to the back surface along an arc of a great circle. The ball hides it from direct view, but strongly deformed images of a short thread segment appear as blue (b) and red (r) ellipses. The label p denotes purple areas. The ball centre is marked by a cross, its perimeter by a dashed line. The enlarged original photograph below is supplied for distance measurements and also traces the red-purple boundary.

The second photograph uses white LED illumination and rotates the ball to show the thread directly:

a
Explain qualitatively, with a ray diagram, why a thread segment is seen as a closed loop in the first photograph.
b
Determine the refractive index \(n_R\) for red light.
c
Determine \(\Delta n=n_V-n_R\), the difference between the violet and red refractive indices.

children.text: T3: Glass ball
a. Two images merging at a fold

For a point \(P\) on the thread and distant camera aperture \(A\), every ray reaching \(A\) lies in plane \(POA\), where \(O\) is the sphere centre. Let \(\alpha\) be the internal incidence angle at the exit surface and \(\beta\) the external angle. Geometry and Snell's law give
\[\gamma=2\alpha-\beta,\qquad n\sin\alpha=\sin\beta.\]

nodes.alt: Original ray diagram in plane POA with centre O, thread point P, two possible exit points Q and Q-prime, distant observer A and the angles alpha, beta, gamma and 2 alpha.

children.text: The function \(\gamma(\alpha)\) is not monotonic. Below its maximum \(\gamma_0\), two exit rays connect a given thread point to the observer. At the maximum the images merge. Thread points outside this accessible range are invisible. The two branches join at their endpoints and form the observed closed oval. A blue shadow marks missing red light and therefore probes the red index.
b. Red refractive index
At the fold, differentiating the two relations gives \(d\beta=2d\alpha\) and \(n\cos\alpha=2\cos\beta\). Combining with Snell's law gives
\[n^2=\sin^2\beta+4\cos^2\beta=4-3\sin^2\beta.\]

c. Dispersion from the oval width

Directly subtracting two nearly equal index estimates has large relative error. Instead measure the blue oval's radial extent \(ST\simeq0.20R\). At the violet fold, red rays from the same thread point have internal angles \(\alpha_R=\alpha_V\pm\delta\), and external angles \(\beta_R=\beta_V\pm2\delta\), because \(\gamma\) is the same. Expand red Snell's law \((n_V-\Delta n)\sin(\alpha_V+\delta)=\sin(\beta_V+2\delta)\) through second order. The first-order terms cancel at the fold, leaving
\[\Delta n=\frac32n_V\delta^2,\qquad \frac{|ST|}{R}\simeq4\delta\cos\beta_V.\]
\[\Delta n\simeq\frac{3n_V}{32}\frac{|ST|^2}{R^2-h^2}\simeq0.0132\simeq0.013.\]

The source's violet-fold reading is approximately \(h/R=0.755\) and \(n_V=1.513\). Use the corresponding violet \(h\) in this width formula. The numerical fields allow the source's stated graph-reading uncertainties, but do not grade the diagram or derivation.
Alternative: solve the paired-ray equations

nodes.alt: Original magnified oval with centre coordinate O, ball edge R and radial ray positions h1, h2, h3 and h4. Red and blue ellipse boundaries are visible against a pixel coordinate scale.

children.text: In the symmetry plane perpendicular to the thread define \(G_n(h)=\arcsin(h/R)-2\arcsin(h/(nR))\). Its non-monotonic dependence on \(h\) gives two images. Solving \(G_{n_R}(h_1)=G_{n_R}(h_4)\) gives \(n_R\simeq1.51\). Then solve \(G_{n_R}(h_{1,4})=G_{n_V}(h_{2,3})\) for all four pairings and average the violet indices. This yields \(n_V-n_R\simeq0.0145\), consistent with the first construction. Both methods and their original partial-credit tables are retained in the PDF.

solution.text:
T3: Glass ball
a. Two images merging at a fold
For a point \(P\) on the thread and distant camera aperture \(A\), every ray reaching \(A\) lies in plane \(POA\), where \(O\) is the sphere centre. Let \(\alpha\) be the internal incidence angle at the exit surface and \(\beta\) the external angle. Geometry and Snell's law give
\[\gamma=2\alpha-\beta,\qquad n\sin\alpha=\sin\beta.\]

The function \(\gamma(\alpha)\) is not monotonic. Below its maximum \(\gamma_0\), two exit rays connect a given thread point to the observer. At the maximum the images merge. Thread points outside this accessible range are invisible. The two branches join at their endpoints and form the observed closed oval. A blue shadow marks missing red light and therefore probes the red index.
b. Red refractive index
At the fold, differentiating the two relations gives \(d\beta=2d\alpha\) and \(n\cos\alpha=2\cos\beta\). Combining with Snell's law gives
\[n^2=\sin^2\beta+4\cos^2\beta=4-3\sin^2\beta.\]

Find the point \(Q_0\) where a radius is tangent to the blue oval. If \(h=OQ_0\), its projected distance gives \(\sin\beta_0=h/R\). The photograph gives \(h/R\simeq0.765\). Thus
\[n_R=\sqrt{4-3(h/R)^2}\simeq1.498\simeq1.50.\]
c. Dispersion from the oval width
Directly subtracting two nearly equal index estimates has large relative error. Instead measure the blue oval's radial extent \(ST\simeq0.20R\). At the violet fold, red rays from the same thread point have internal angles \(\alpha_R=\alpha_V\pm\delta\), and external angles \(\beta_R=\beta_V\pm2\delta\), because \(\gamma\) is the same. Expand red Snell's law \((n_V-\Delta n)\sin(\alpha_V+\delta)=\sin(\beta_V+2\delta)\) through second order. The first-order terms cancel at the fold, leaving
\[\Delta n=\frac32n_V\delta^2,\qquad \frac{|ST|}{R}\simeq4\delta\cos\beta_V.\]
\[\Delta n\simeq\frac{3n_V}{32}\frac{|ST|^2}{R^2-h^2}\simeq0.0132\simeq0.013.\]
The source's violet-fold reading is approximately \(h/R=0.755\) and \(n_V=1.513\). Use the corresponding violet \(h\) in this width formula. The numerical fields allow the source's stated graph-reading uncertainties, but do not grade the diagram or derivation.
Alternative: solve the paired-ray equations

In the symmetry plane perpendicular to the thread define \(G_n(h)=\arcsin(h/R)-2\arcsin(h/(nR))\). Its non-monotonic dependence on \(h\) gives two images. Solving \(G_{n_R}(h_1)=G_{n_R}(h_4)\) gives \(n_R\simeq1.51\). Then solve \(G_{n_R}(h_{1,4})=G_{n_V}(h_{2,3})\) for all four pairings and average the violet indices. This yields \(n_V-n_R\simeq0.0145\), consistent with the first construction. Both methods and their original partial-credit tables are retained in the PDF.
